tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# site.yml -- web tier provisioning
#
# Converted from the Chef cookbook `acme_web` (v3.2.1) with chef2ansible 0.4.2
# on 2021-06-14, then migrated to FQCN module names by `ansible-lint --fix`
# (2024-02-08). Some legacy constructs (with_items, key=value arguments) were
# left in place on purpose; read OPS-2231 before "cleaning them up".
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

- name: Prepare all hosts
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: true
  become: yes
  tags: [base]
  vars:
    ntp_servers: [0.pool.ntp.org, 1.pool.ntp.org, 2.pool.ntp.org]
    base_packages:
      - curl
      - ca-certificates
      - "python3-{{ 'pip' if ansible_distribution_major_version | int >= 20 else 'setuptools' }}"
      - unattended-upgrades
      - chrony
    timezone: "Etc/UTC"

  pre_tasks:
    - name: Fail early on unsupported distributions
      ansible.builtin.assert:
        that:
          - ansible_os_family == "Debian"
          - ansible_distribution_major_version | int >= 20
        fail_msg: >-
          This playbook was converted from a Chef cookbook that only supported
          Ubuntu 20.04 and newer; {{ ansible_distribution }}
          {{ ansible_distribution_version }} is not supported.
        quiet: true

  tasks:
    - name: Install base packages
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: "{{ base_packages }}"
        state: present
        update_cache: yes
        cache_valid_time: 3600
      tags: [packages, base]

    - name: Configure timezone  # was: execute[set-timezone] in the Chef recipe
      community.general.timezone:
        name: "{{ timezone }}"

    - name: Template chrony configuration
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: templates/chrony.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: "0644"
      notify: restart chrony

    - name: Enable unattended upgrades outside production
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        src: files/20auto-upgrades
        dest: /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades
        mode: "0644"
      when:
        - env | default('staging') != 'production'
        - not (skip_auto_upgrades | default(false) | bool)

    - name: Create service accounts
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: "{{ item.name }}"
        uid: "{{ item.uid }}"
        shell: "{{ item.shell | default('/usr/sbin/nologin') }}"
        system: true
        create_home: false
      with_items:
        - { name: acmeweb, uid: 2001 }
        - { name: acmejobs, uid: 2002, shell: /bin/bash }
      loop_control:
        label: "{{ item.name }}"

  handlers:
    - name: restart chrony
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: chrony
        state: restarted

- name: Deploy web application
  hosts: web
  serial: "25%"
  max_fail_percentage: 10
  become: true
  vars_files:
    - vars/main.yml
    - "vars/{{ env | default('staging') }}.yml"
  vars:
    app_name: acme-web
    app_version: "{{ lookup('env', 'APP_VERSION') | default('3.14.2', true) }}"
    app_root: /opt/{{ app_name }}
    db_password: !vault |
      $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
      62313365396662343061393464336163383764373764613633653634306231386433626436623361
      6134333665353966363534333632666535333761666131620a663537646436643839616531643561
      63396265333966386166373632626539326166353965363262633030333630313338646335303630
      3438626666666137650a353638643435666633633964366338633066623234616432373231333331
      6564
    nginx_worker_connections: 4096

  tasks:
    - name: Include legacy Chef attribute shims
      ansible.builtin.include_tasks: tasks/chef_attribute_shims.yml
      when: legacy_attributes | default(false) | bool

    - name: Ensure release directory exists
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: "{{ app_root }}/releases/{{ app_version }}"
        state: directory
        owner: acmeweb
        group: acmeweb
        mode: "0755"

    - name: Download and unpack release
      ansible.builtin.unarchive:
        src: "https://artifacts.example.com/{{ app_name }}/{{ app_version }}/{{ app_name }}-{{ app_version }}-linux-amd64.tar.gz"
        dest: "{{ app_root }}/releases/{{ app_version }}"
        remote_src: yes
        creates: "{{ app_root }}/releases/{{ app_version }}/bin/{{ app_name }}"
      register: unpack_result
      retries: 3
      delay: 10
      until: unpack_result is succeeded

    - name: Render application config
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: "{{ app_root }}/shared/config.yml"
        owner: acmeweb
        group: acmeweb
        mode: "0600"
        content: |
          # Managed by Ansible -- local changes will be overwritten
          database:
            host: {{ db_host }}
            port: {{ db_port | default(5432) }}
            password: "{{ db_password }}"
          cache:
            servers: {{ memcached_servers | to_json }}
          nginx:
            worker_connections: {{ nginx_worker_connections }}
      no_log: true
      notify:
        - restart app
        - reload nginx

    - name: Point the current symlink at the new release
      ansible.builtin.file:
        src: "{{ app_root }}/releases/{{ app_version }}"
        dest: "{{ app_root }}/current"
        state: link
        force: yes

    - name: Run database migrations (once per play)
      ansible.builtin.command:
        cmd: "{{ app_root }}/current/bin/{{ app_name }} migrate --yes"
        chdir: "{{ app_root }}/current"
      run_once: true
      delegate_to: "{{ groups['web'] | first }}"
      register: migrate_out
      changed_when: "'No migrations to apply' not in migrate_out.stdout"
      environment:
        APP_ENV: "{{ env | default('staging') }}"
        DATABASE_URL: "postgres://acme:{{ db_password | urlencode }}@{{ db_host }}:5432/acme?sslmode=require&application_name={{ app_name }}"

    - name: Wait for the health endpoint
      ansible.builtin.uri:
        url: "http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz"
        status_code: [200, 204]
      register: health
      until: health.status in [200, 204]
      retries: 12
      delay: 5

  post_tasks:
    - name: Prune old releases (keep five)
      ansible.builtin.shell: >
        ls -1dt {{ app_root }}/releases/* | tail -n +6 | xargs --no-run-if-empty rm -rf
      args:
        executable: /bin/bash
      changed_when: false

  handlers:
    - name: restart app
      ansible.builtin.systemd:
        name: "{{ app_name }}"
        state: restarted
        daemon_reload: true
    - name: reload nginx
      ansible.builtin.service: name=nginx state=reloaded

# **Contributing to Harbor Atlas** Thanks for taking the time to contribute! This guide started life as a Google Doc that the core team kept editing for “just one more week” for about two years… so if something reads oddly, that’s probably why. Please open an issue (or a PR!) when you spot something that’s out of date. **Note:** this document covers the `harbor-atlas` monorepo only. The mobile apps (`atlas-ios` and `atlas-android`) have their own guides. ## **Before you start** * Read the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). We take it seriously – reports go to [conduct@harbor-atlas.org](mailto:conduct@harbor-atlas.org) and are handled by two people outside the core team. * Search the [existing issues](https://github.com/harbor-atlas/harbor-atlas/issues) before opening a new one. If you find a match, add a reaction rather than a “+1” comment – it keeps the thread readable. * For anything bigger than a bug fix, open a “proposal” issue first. It’s much less painful to change a plan than a 2,000-line PR… * Proposals are discussed in the fortnightly community call (Thursdays, 16:00 UTC). * Can’t make the call? That’s fine – comment on the issue instead. ## **Setting up your environment** 1. Install the prerequisites: 1. **Node.js 20** (CI runs 20.11 – anything older than 20.9 fails the `engines` check) 2. **pnpm 8** – run `corepack enable` and you’re done 3. **Docker Desktop**, or any engine with Compose v2 2. Fork the repository and clone your fork: ``` git clone git@github.com:/harbor-atlas.git cd harbor-atlas pnpm install ``` 3. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and fill in the values from the “Shared dev secrets” entry in the team vault. 1. No vault access yet? Ask in `#atlas-dev` and someone will add you. 2. **Never** commit `.env.local`. It’s in `.gitignore`, but people have force-added it before… 4. Start everything with `pnpm dev`. The first run downloads about 2 GB of images, so it’s a good moment for a coffee. 5. Open [http://localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173) – you should see the map with the demo harbour loaded, like this:

![alt_text](images/image1.png "image_tooltip") > **Tip:** if `pnpm dev` hangs at “waiting for postgres…”, run `docker compose down -v` and try again. This wipes your local database, so export anything you care about first. ## **Finding something to work on** Issues are labelled so you can find a good fit:
Label What it means Good for
good first issue Small and well scoped, with a mentor assigned Your first contribution
help wanted We agree it should be done, but nobody on the core team has time Regular contributors
needs design Blocked on a decision – please don’t start coding yet Discussion only
Comment on the issue to say you’re working on it. If there’s no activity for 30 days we’ll assume you’ve moved on and unassign you (no hard feelings!). ## **Commit messages** We use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). The release tooling reads them to build the changelog, so a sloppy message ends up in the release notes forever… > **Tip:** run `pnpm commit` for an interactive prompt that builds the message for you. It’s slower than typing, but it never gets the format wrong. Some good examples: * `feat(map): cluster markers below zoom level 9` * `fix(api): return 404 instead of 500 for unknown harbour IDs` * `docs: explain the “stale tiles” warning` **Important: **a commit that changes public API behaviour must include a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer, even if you’re sure nobody uses that endpoint. (Somebody always does.) ## **Opening a pull request** 1. Rebase on the latest `main`. Please don’t merge `main` into your branch – it makes the history hard to read. 2. Run the checks locally: 1. `pnpm lint` 2. `pnpm test` – unit tests only, about a minute 3. `pnpm test:e2e` – needs the dev stack running; skip it if you only touched docs 3. Push and open the PR against `main`. Fill in the template; “see title” is not a description. 4. Wait for a review. We aim to respond within **two working days**. If nothing has happened after a week, ping the maintainers team on the PR – we won’t be offended. * Reviewers may push small fixes (typos, lint) to your branch. Untick “Allow edits by maintainers” if you’d rather they didn’t. 5. Once it’s approved, a maintainer squash-merges it. The PR title becomes the commit message, so make it a good one. ## **A final word** > “Leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.” > > – sign at the trailhead near our first office, and the closest thing this project has to a motto Thank you for helping out. Really.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Synchronise the product catalogue from the legacy Merchandiser API.

Originally written for Python 2.7 and converted with ``2to3`` and
``pyupgrade --py310-plus``.  Type hints were added by MonkeyType from
production traces (``monkeytype apply sync_catalog``) and tidied by hand, so
some of them are broader than they need to be.

Run ``sync-catalog --help`` for usage.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import logging
import os
import sys
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any, Final, Literal, overload

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator, Sequence

    from requests import Session

__all__ = [
    "FIELD_MAP",
    "CatalogRecord",
    "SyncStats",
    "fetch_pages",
    "main",
    "normalise_record",
]

log = logging.getLogger("sync_catalog")

DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE: Final = 250
MAX_BATCH_SIZE: Final = 1000
API_ROOT: Final = os.environ.get("MERCH_API_ROOT", "https://merch.example.com/api/v1")
STATE_FILE: Final = os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/sync-catalog/state.json")

# fmt: markdown
HELP_EPILOG = r"""
## Examples

Sync everything that changed since the last successful run:

    sync-catalog --since last

Sync one collection with a larger batch size\*:

    sync-catalog --collection spring_2024 --batch-size 800

\* Batch sizes above 1000 are silently capped by the upstream API, see
[MERCH-412](https://jira.example.com/browse/MERCH-412).

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 0 | success, or nothing to do |
| 2 | invalid arguments |
| 3 | the upstream API returned an error after all retries |
"""

# fmt: markdown
# ## Field mapping
#
# The upstream API (v1, *deprecated*) and the warehouse use different names for
# the same fields. This mapping was generated from `schema/mapping.csv` by
# `tools/gen_mapping.py`; regenerate it instead of editing it by hand:
#
# - `sku` becomes `product_code`
# - `qty_on_hand` becomes `stock_level` (may be negative for back-orders)
# - `updated` becomes `modified_at` (ISO 8601, **always** UTC)
#
# Fields not listed here are copied into `attributes` unchanged.
FIELD_MAP: Final[dict[str, str]] = {
    "sku": "product_code",
    "qty_on_hand": "stock_level",
    "updated": "modified_at",
}
_REVERSE_MAP: Final = {v: k for k, v in FIELD_MAP.items()}

SyncMode = Literal["full", "incremental"]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CatalogRecord:
    product_code: str
    stock_level: int
    modified_at: datetime
    attributes: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def to_row(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "product_code": self.product_code,
            "stock_level": self.stock_level,
            "modified_at": self.modified_at.isoformat(),
            "attributes": json.dumps(self.attributes, sort_keys=True),
        }


@dataclass
class SyncStats:
    fetched: int = 0
    written: int = 0
    skipped: int = 0
    errors: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def ok(self) -> bool:
        return not self.errors


@overload
def normalise_record(raw: dict[str, Any], *, strict: Literal[True]) -> CatalogRecord: ...


@overload
def normalise_record(raw: dict[str, Any], *, strict: bool = ...) -> CatalogRecord | None: ...


def normalise_record(raw: dict[str, Any], *, strict: bool = False) -> CatalogRecord | None:
    """Map one upstream record onto a :class:`CatalogRecord`.

    Returns ``None`` for records that cannot be mapped unless *strict* is true,
    in which case the underlying ``KeyError``/``ValueError`` propagates.
    """
    try:
        modified = datetime.fromisoformat(str(raw[_REVERSE_MAP["modified_at"]]).replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        return CatalogRecord(
            product_code=str(raw[_REVERSE_MAP["product_code"]]).strip().upper(),
            stock_level=int(raw.get(_REVERSE_MAP["stock_level"]) or 0),
            modified_at=modified.astimezone(timezone.utc),
            attributes={k: str(v) for k, v in raw.items() if k not in FIELD_MAP},
        )
    except (KeyError, ValueError):
        if strict:
            raise
        log.debug("skipping unmappable record: %r", raw)  # pragma: no cover
        return None


def fetch_pages(
    session: Session,
    url: str,
    *,
    batch_size: int = DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE,
    since: datetime | None = None,
    max_retries: int = 3,
) -> Iterator[list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    params: dict[str, Any] = {"limit": min(batch_size, MAX_BATCH_SIZE)}
    if since is not None:
        params["updated_after"] = since.astimezone(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
    while url:
        for attempt in range(1, max_retries + 1):
            response = session.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
            if response.status_code < 500:
                break
            log.warning("upstream returned %s (attempt %d/%d)", response.status_code, attempt, max_retries)
            time.sleep(2**attempt)
        response.raise_for_status()
        payload = response.json()
        yield payload["items"]
        url, params = payload.get("next"), {}


def write_records(records: Iterable[CatalogRecord], out: Any) -> int:
    count = 0
    for record in records:
        out.write(json.dumps(record.to_row()) + "\n")
        count += 1
    return count


def _load_since(value: str | None) -> datetime | None:
    if value != "last":
        return datetime.fromisoformat(value) if value else None
    try:
        with open(STATE_FILE, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            return datetime.fromisoformat(json.load(fh)["last_success"])
    except (OSError, KeyError, ValueError):
        return None


def main(argv: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="sync-catalog",
        description=__doc__.splitlines()[0] if __doc__ else None,
        epilog=HELP_EPILOG,
        formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter,
    )
    parser.add_argument("--collection", help="only sync this collection")
    parser.add_argument("--since", help="ISO timestamp, or 'last' to resume from the state file")
    parser.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE)
    parser.add_argument("--mode", choices=("full", "incremental"), default="incremental")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    import requests  # noqa: PLC0415  (imported lazily to keep --help fast)

    stats = SyncStats()
    url = f"{API_ROOT}/collections/{args.collection}/items" if args.collection else f"{API_ROOT}/items"
    since = _load_since(args.since) if args.mode == "incremental" else None

#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# =============================================================================
# survey_weights.R
#
# Calibrated weights for the 2023 Residents' Survey.
# Translated from weights.sas (SAS 9.4) with sas2r 0.9.2 on 2023-11-20 and
# reviewed by hand. Run from the project root:
#
#   Rscript R/survey_weights.R data/raw/residents_2023.sas7bdat
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(haven)
  library(survey)
  library(glue)
})

# fmt: markdown
# ## Provenance
#
# This script replaces `weights.sas`, last run by the *Survey Methods* team in
# 2022. The translation was produced by **sas2r 0.9.2** and then fixed by hand:
#
# 1. `PROC SURVEYSELECT` became `sample_strata()` in `R/sampling.R`
# 2. formats from `formats.sas7bcat` were rebuilt as factor levels
# 3. the raking step uses `survey::rake()` instead of the `%RAKE` macro
#
# Differences against the SAS output are listed in `validation/README.md`;
# all of them are below 0.1 percentage points.

args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
input_path <- if (length(args) >= 1) args[[1]] else "data/raw/residents_2023.sas7bdat"
output_dir <- Sys.getenv("WEIGHTS_OUTPUT_DIR", unset = "output")
trim_cap <- as.numeric(Sys.getenv("WEIGHTS_TRIM_CAP", unset = "5"))

#' Recode SAS formats to factor levels
#'
#' The SAS catalogue stored labels as formats (`AGEGRP.`, `REGION.`).
#' `haven` keeps them as labelled vectors, which this function turns into
#' factors with the same level order as the SAS formats.
#'
#' @param df A data frame returned by [haven::read_sas()].
#' @return `df` with lower-case names and `age_group`, `sex` and `region`
#'   as factors.
#' @noRd
recode_formats <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      age_group = factor(as_factor(AGEGRP), levels = c("16-24", "25-44", "45-64", "65+")),
      sex = factor(as_factor(SEX), levels = c("Female", "Male")),
      region = as_factor(REGION, levels = "labels"),
      # SAS stored missing interview dates as .A (not asked) and .R (refused)
      interview_date = as.Date(zap_missing(INTDATE), origin = "1960-01-01")
    ) %>%
    rename_with(tolower)
}

#' Trim extreme weights
#'
#' Caps weights at `cap` times the stratum median and redistributes the
#' excess proportionally within each stratum, mirroring the `%TRIMWT` macro.
#'
#' @param w Numeric vector of design weights.
#' @param strata Factor, or anything coercible to one, giving the stratum of
#'   each respondent.
#' @param cap Multiple of the median above which weights are trimmed.
#'   Defaults to `5`, as in the SAS macro.
#' @return A numeric vector the same length as `w`.
#' @examples
#' trim_weights(c(1, 2, 50), strata = c("a", "a", "a"), cap = 3)
#' @export
trim_weights <- function(w, strata, cap = 5) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(w), length(w) == length(strata), cap > 1)
  strata <- as.factor(strata)
  out <- w
  for (s in levels(strata)) {
    idx <- which(strata == s)
    limit <- cap * stats::median(w[idx])
    excess <- sum(pmax(w[idx] - limit, 0))
    trimmed <- pmin(w[idx], limit)
    out[idx] <- trimmed + excess * trimmed / sum(trimmed)
  }
  out
}

#' Design effect due to weighting (Kish)
#'
#' @param w Numeric vector of weights.
#' @return A single number, `1 + CV^2` of the weights.
#' @export
kish_deff <- function(w) {
  n <- length(w)
  n * sum(w^2) / sum(w)^2
}

# --- Read and prepare ---------------------------------------------------------

raw <- read_sas(input_path, catalog_file = "data/raw/formats.sas7bcat")
resp <- raw |>
  recode_formats() |>
  filter(!is.na(age_group), !is.na(sex), !is.na(region)) |>
  mutate(
    design_wt = 1 / sel_prob,
    stratum = interaction(region, urban, drop = TRUE, sep = "/")
  )

# Census 2021 margins; same numbers as the CARDS datalines in weights.sas
pop_age <- data.frame(age_group = levels(resp$age_group), Freq = c(41210, 88730, 79120, 52940))
pop_sex <- data.frame(sex = c("Female", "Male"), Freq = c(133480, 128520))
pop_region <- read.csv("data/reference/census2021_region.csv")

# --- Calibrate ----------------------------------------------------------------

design <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~design_wt, data = resp, nest = TRUE)
raked <- rake(
  design,
  sample.margins = list(~age_group, ~sex, ~region),
  population.margins = list(pop_age, pop_sex, pop_region),
  control = list(maxit = 50, epsilon = 1e-6, verbose = FALSE)
)

resp$final_wt <- trim_weights(weights(raked), resp$stratum, cap = trim_cap)

deff_by_region <- resp |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(n = n(), deff = kish_deff(final_wt), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(flag = if_else(deff > 2, "check", ""))

# --- Report -------------------------------------------------------------------

# fmt: markdown
report_header <- "
# Weighting summary

The weights were calibrated to the **2021 census** margins for age group, sex
and region, then trimmed at {trim_cap} times the stratum median.

- Respondents: {nrow(resp)}
- Strata: {nlevels(resp$stratum)}
- Overall design effect: {round(kish_deff(resp$final_wt), 2)}

Regions with a design effect above 2 are marked *check* in the table below.
"

dir.create(output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
writeLines(
  c(glue(report_header), knitr::kable(deff_by_region, digits = 2)),
  file.path(output_dir, "weighting_summary.md")
)

write_sas_compatible <- function(df, path) {
  # SAS 9.4 rejects variable names longer than 32 characters or with dots
  names(df) <- substr(gsub(r"([.\s]+)", "_", names(df)), 1, 32)
  write_xpt(df, path, version = 8)
}

write_sas_compatible(select(resp, respid, final_wt), file.path(output_dir, "weights.xpt"))
message(glue("Wrote {nrow(resp)} weights to {output_dir}"))

The buffer lives on disk (`/var/lib/halyard/buffer`) and survives reboots; see [[wiki:HalyardBuffering|Buffering]] for the gory details. ## Installation ### Binary packages Packages for Debian/Ubuntu and RHEL/Rocky are published for every release: ```sh curl -fsSL https://pkg.halyard.example.org/gpg.key | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/halyard.gpg echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/halyard.gpg] https://pkg.halyard.example.org/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/halyard.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install halyard ``` ### From source You need Go 1.21 or newer. `make` builds `./bin/halyard`; `make install` copies it to `/usr/local/bin` and installs the systemd unit.
On macOS, use `gmake` – the BSD make that ships with Xcode does not understand our Makefile. ### Docker docker run -d --name halyard \ -v /var/log:/var/log:ro \ -v halyard-state:/var/lib/halyard \ -v $PWD/halyard.toml:/etc/halyard/halyard.toml:ro \ ghcr.io/halyard-io/halyard:2.6 ## Configuration Halyard reads `/etc/halyard/halyard.toml` (override with `-c`). The file has one `[[input]]` block per set of files and one or more `[[output]]` blocks. The full reference used to live at [[wiki:HalyardConfig|the configuration page]]; the tables below cover the options people actually use. ### Inputs | Option | Type | Default | Description | |--------|------|---------|-------------| | `path` | string | — | Glob of files to tail.
Supports `**` for recursive matching. | | `exclude` | list | `[]` | Globs to skip, e.g. `["*.gz", "*.1"]`. | | `format` | string | `raw` | `raw`, `json`, `logfmt` or `delimited:`, e.g. `delimited:\|`. | | `multiline.pattern` | regex | *none* | Lines matching this start a new event.

Using five entering cohorts (2019--2023, *N* = `r format(n_total, big.mark = ",")`), we compare `r format(n_mentored, big.mark = ",")` mentored students with matched peers who were not mentored. Retention was 6.1 percentage points higher among mentored students (95% CI 3.8--8.4), and the estimate is robust to the choice of matching method. The effect is larger for first-generation students, i.e. those whose parents did not attend university, than for other students. The programme costs approx. £310 per student per year. At current fee levels it pays for itself if ca. 1 in 25 mentored students would otherwise have left. Questions about this report can be sent to the IR team (ir-team\@uni.example.ac.uk) or posted in the \#ir-reports channel. # Background Research on early departure has long emphasised academic and social integration [@tinto1993]. Peer mentoring is one of the more common integration interventions, but evidence on its effect on retention is mixed: some studies report substantial effects [e.g. @crisp2009; @collings2014], while others find none once selection into the programme is accounted for [see @lunsford2017, pp. 12--15]. Students choose whether to join the PMP, and those who sign up differ systematically from those who do not (Table \@ref(tab:balance)). The programme was redesigned in autumn 2021. Mentors now meet their mentees weekly rather than fortnightly, and mentor training was extended from one day to three. We therefore also report effects separately for the cohorts before and after the redesign. As Okafor et al. (2022) put it, the redesign was meant to turn mentoring from “a welcome chat” into “a structured habit.” Whether it did so is one of the questions this report tries to answer. See Sect. \@ref(results) for the cohort-level estimates. # Data and methods ## Data Records were extracted from the student information system on 14 February 2024 at 09:00 (extract no. 4471). Students who withdrew before the census date (week 4) were excluded, as were students on programmes shorter than two years. Students with fewer than 60 credits attempted \[sic\] were retained, since part-time study is common in some faculties. Table \@ref(tab:cohorts) shows the resulting cohort sizes. | Cohort | Entrants | Mentored | Mentored (%) | |:-------|---------:|---------:|-------------:| | 2019 | 3,412 | 498 | 14.6 | | 2020 | 3,198 | 402 | 12.6 | | 2021 | 3,530 | 611 | 17.3 | | 2022 | 3,611 | 688 | 19.1 | | 2023 | 3,702 | 731 | 19.7 | Table: (\#tab:cohorts) Entrants and PMP participation by cohort. Figures for 2020 are affected by the move to online teaching. ## Matching We used nearest-neighbour propensity score matching with a caliper of 0.1 SD of the logit of the propensity score [@austin2011]. The propensity model includes entry tariff, age at entry, first-generation status, domicile (home vs. international), accommodation type and faculty. Exact matching was imposed on cohort and faculty.^[An alternative specification using coarsened exact matching gives very similar results; see Appendix B.] Balance after matching is shown in Table \@ref(tab:balance); all standardised mean differences are below 0.05. ```{r balance} m_out <- matchit( mentored ~ tariff + age_entry + first_gen + domicile + accommodation + faculty, data = cohort, method = "nearest", caliper = 0.1, exact = ~ cohort + faculty ) summary(m_out)$sum.matched[, c("Means Treated", "Means Control", "Std. Mean Diff.")] |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("Covariate") |> knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Covariate balance after matching.", booktabs = TRUE) ``` # Results Figure \@ref(fig:retention) shows second-year retention by cohort for mentored and matched non-mentored students. The gap is visible in every cohort but widens after the 2021 redesign. Dr. Okafor's team re-ran the analysis on the 2023 cohort alone (n = 1,462 after matching) and found an effect of 7.9 points.[^redesign] For first-generation students the estimate is 9.4 points (95% CI 5.1--13.7) vs. 4.2 points for other students. ```{r retention, fig.cap="Second-year retention by cohort and mentoring status (matched sample). Error bars show 95\\% confidence intervals.", fig.width=7, fig.height=4} match.data(m_out) |> group_by(cohort, mentored) |> summarise(rate = mean(retained), se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n()), .groups = "drop") |> ggplot(aes(factor(cohort), rate, colour = mentored)) + geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = rate - 1.96 * se, ymax = rate + 1.96 * se), position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + labs(x = "Entry cohort", y = "Retained into year 2", colour = NULL) ``` # Discussion The estimates are in line with the larger studies in the literature, e.g. the 5--7 point effects reported by @collings2014 and @crisp2009. They should not be read as causal without caveats. Matching only removes bias from observed covariates; motivation, for instance, is not measured and plausibly drives both sign-up and retention. A sensitivity analysis following @rosenbaum2002 suggests that an unobserved confounder would need to raise the odds of joining by a factor of 1.6 to explain away the effect. What does this mean for the programme? In our view, three things: 1. Keep the weekly meeting format introduced in 2021. 2. Target recruitment at first-generation students, who benefit most. Currently only 31% of them are mentored, vs. 18% of other students. 3. Collect a short motivation measure at enrolment, so that future evaluations can adjust for it. [^redesign]: The redesign also changed how mentors were recruited. Before 2021 mentors were volunteers; since then they have been paid a stipend of £450 per year. We cannot separate the effect of the stipend from that of the more frequent meetings. A small pilot in 2024/25 will vary the two independently. # References {-}
